ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

ask.changes_what: Positive: trial withdrawal/dose reduction and reassess, check creatinine; negative or non-resolving: pursue HF, venous, renal, hepatic and DVT causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not label edema as drug-induced when there is dyspnea, orthopnea, elevated JVP, unilateral swelling, hypoalbuminemia/proteinuria or rising creatinine until those causes are evaluated.
ask.escalation_warning: Thiazolidinedione- or NSAID-associated edema with weight gain and dyspnea may be new/worsened heart failure; NSAID edema with oliguria or rising creatinine indicates AKI - stop the drug and assess urgently.
ask.how: Review the full list for dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine), NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, corticosteroids, direct vasodilators (minoxidil, hydralazine), estrogens/progestins, testosterone, docetaxel, and DPP-4 or insulin. Record start date and dose escalation relative to edema onset and whether edema is bilateral, dependent and non-tender.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug makes medication effect unlikely and directs evaluation toward heart failure, venous insufficiency, renal/hepatic disease or DVT (if unilateral).
ask.pitfalls: Up to one-third of edema on amlodipine is not caused by it, and thiazolidinediones/NSAIDs can precipitate true heart failure rather than benign edema; drug edema is a diagnosis of exclusion when JVP, BNP or echo suggest cardiac disease. Unilateral or painful edema is never attributed to medication.
ask.positive_finding: Bilateral dependent edema beginning weeks after starting or increasing a dihydropyridine CCB, NSAID, thiazolidinedione, gabapentinoid, steroid or vasodilator, without orthopnea, elevated JVP or weight gain out of proportion, supports drug-induced edema (and NSAIDs also cause AKI/sodium retention).
ask.prerequisites: Reconciled medication list including over-the-counter NSAIDs; weight trend, orthopnea/PND and JVP assessment to distinguish drug edema from heart failure.
ask.title: Medication review for edema: dihydropyridine CCB, NSAIDs, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, steroids, minoxidil/hydralazine

ask.changes_what: New orthopnoea raises probability of decompensated HF and supports BNP/echo and decongestion; absence should not be used to exclude HF.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on the absence of orthopnoea to exclude heart failure, and do not attribute orthopnoea to heart failure without examining for tamponade, effusion or neuromuscular weakness when the picture does not fit.
ask.escalation_warning: Orthopnoea with hypotension, pulsus paradoxus or a raised JVP suggests tamponade or acute pump failure; obtain immediate echo.

evidence.citation: Fonseca C, Morais H, Mota T, et al. The diagnosis of heart failure in primary care: value of symptoms and signs. Eur J Heart Fail. 2004;6(6):795-800.
evidence.population: Portuguese primary care attendees screened by Boston questionnaire and referred for echocardiography (n=1058 assessed); orthopnoea sensitivity reported only as <36%
evidence.quote: a history of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (LR 35.5), orthopnea (LR 39.1) and breathlessness when walking on the flat (LR 25.8)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (cardiac dysfunction at rest on echocardiography)

evidence.citation: Ekundayo OJ, Howard VJ, Safford MM, et al. Value of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and medications in prospective population studies of incident heart failure. Am J Cardiol. 2009;104(2):259-264.
evidence.population: 5,771 community-dwelling adults >=65 years in the Cardiovascular Health Study; 272 with adjudicated definite HF
evidence.quote: for either orthopnea or PND were 52% (95% confidence interval [CI] 46% to 58%), 83% (95% CI 82% to 84%)
evidence.reference_standard: Centrally adjudicated definite heart failure (CHS criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Prevalent definite heart failure (composite symptom: orthopnoea OR paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea)

ask.how: Ask whether breathing worsens within minutes of lying flat and eases on sitting up, how many pillows (or what head-of-bed angle) are needed to sleep, and whether this is new or increased compared with baseline. Distinguish from positional dyspnoea due to abdominal distension, obesity, or nasal obstruction, and from cough-related waking.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of orthopnoea only modestly lowers the probability of heart failure; many heart failure patients, particularly with chronic disease, sleep flat.
ask.pitfalls: Orthopnoea also occurs with COPD, massive ascites, obesity, and bilateral diaphragm paralysis; pillow count is confounded by habit, reflux and sinus disease. In chronic HF orthopnoea correlates poorly with measured wedge pressure.
ask.positive_finding: New or worsening need to sleep propped up, with dyspnoea on lying flat that resolves on sitting, points to raised left-sided filling pressure (heart failure) or, less often, tamponade, large effusion or bilateral diaphragm weakness.
ask.prerequisites: Patient (or collateral historian) able to describe sleep position and recent change.
ask.title: Orthopnea: dyspnea lying flat relieved by sitting up / number of pillows

ask.changes_what: PND raises probability of decompensated HF (pooled LR+ ~2.6 in ED) and supports BNP/echo; absence changes little.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of PND to exclude heart failure; do not label nocturnal wheeze as asthma in an older patient with risk factors for heart failure without checking for congestion.
ask.escalation_warning: PND with chest pain, new oedema or hypoxaemia at rest indicates decompensation that needs same-day assessment rather than outpatient follow-up.

evidence.quote: the symptom of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (positive LR = 2.6; 95% CI, 1.5-4.5)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of heart failure adjudicated in the primary studies (varied criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnoea

evidence.population: 5,771 community-dwelling adults >=65 years in the Cardiovascular Health Study; 272 with adjudicated definite HF
evidence.quote: for either orthopnea or PND were 52% (95% confidence interval [CI] 46% to 58%), 83% (95% CI 82% to 84%)

ask.how: Ask whether the patient wakes from sleep, typically 1-3 hours after lying down, gasping or short of breath and has to sit up, stand or go to a window for relief that takes 10-30 minutes. Ask about wheeze or cough with the episodes and about daytime exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and oedema to separate cardiac from asthmatic nocturnal symptoms.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of PND is common in heart failure and provides little reassurance; it should not lower the probability enough to stop the work-up.
ask.pitfalls: Nocturnal asthma, COPD with secretions, sleep apnoea, reflux/aspiration and nocturnal angina produce similar waking; 'cardiac asthma' with wheeze is easily mislabelled as asthma. Recall is unreliable and prevalence is low so specificity drives its value.
ask.positive_finding: Episodes of waking from sleep with dyspnoea that resolve slowly on sitting or standing indicate redistribution of fluid into the lungs from raised left-sided filling pressure, i.e. decompensated heart failure.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or bed partner able to describe nocturnal episodes.
ask.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: waking 1-3 h after sleep with dyspnea relieved by sitting/standing

examine.changes_what: Positive: adds 1 Wells point and pushes toward compression ultrasound; negative does not stop work-up if other Wells items or D-dimer are positive.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm calf compression if DVT is strongly suspected and pain is severe.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative calf measurement to withhold imaging in a patient with moderate/high Wells probability or with symptoms suggesting PE.
examine.escalation_warning: Massive swelling with cyanosis or pallor and pain (phlegmasia) or a cold pulseless limb requires immediate vascular imaging and consultation.

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: the value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
evidence.population: Patients with clinically suspected DVT (cohort studies comparing clinical assessment with a reference standard; pooled random-effects)
evidence.quote: malignancy (likelihood ratio [LR], 2.71), previous DVT (LR, 2.25), recent immobilization (LR, 1.98), difference in calf diameter (LR, 1.80)
evidence.reference_standard: Venography or compression/duplex ultrasound (study-specific reference standard)
evidence.target_condition: DVT (finding: difference in calf diameter, present)

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: the value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
evidence.population: Patients with clinically suspected DVT (cohort studies comparing clinical assessment with a reference standard; pooled random-effects)
evidence.quote: absence of calf swelling (LR, 0.67) or difference in calf diameter (LR, 0.57) was useful for ruling out DVT
evidence.reference_standard: Venography or compression/duplex ultrasound (study-specific reference standard)
evidence.target_condition: DVT (finding: difference in calf diameter, absent)

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: the value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
evidence.population: Patients with clinically suspected DVT (cohort studies comparing clinical assessment with a reference standard; pooled random-effects)
evidence.quote: absence of calf swelling (LR, 0.67) or difference in calf diameter (LR, 0.57) was useful for ruling out DVT
evidence.reference_standard: Venography or compression/duplex ultrasound (study-specific reference standard)
evidence.target_condition: DVT (finding: calf swelling, absent)

examine.how: With the patient supine and legs relaxed, mark a point 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity on each leg and measure calf circumference with a tape at the same level bilaterally. A difference >3 cm (symptomatic side larger) is positive; also note localized tenderness along the deep venous system and pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg.
examine.negative_finding: No calf-diameter difference (LR- 0.57) or no calf swelling (LR- 0.67) lowers the probability of DVT only modestly; it cannot exclude DVT on its own.
examine.pitfalls: Chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema, cellulitis, Baker cyst, and prior DVT produce asymmetry without acute thrombosis; measuring at different levels or in a dependent leg creates spurious differences. Calf tenderness alone has LR near 1.
examine.positive_finding: Calf-diameter difference roughly doubles the odds of DVT (pooled LR+ 1.8); it is the only physical sign with useful rule-in value but is far weaker than the overall Wells score (high probability LR 5.2).
examine.prerequisites: Both legs accessible and comparable (no prior amputation, cast, or chronic unilateral disease that already explains asymmetry).
examine.title: Unilateral leg swelling: calf circumference difference >3 cm (10 cm below tibial tuberosity), with calf tenderness

examine.changes_what: Unilateral warm erythema: treat as cellulitis but rule out DVT/necrotizing infection; bilateral: seek pseudocellulitis (stasis, dermatitis) before antibiotics.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use asymmetry/border to reassure when there is severe pain, rapid progression, bullae, crepitus, hypotension or immunocompromise; necrotizing infection needs surgical evaluation regardless of score.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral swollen warm leg also fits DVT: obtain compression ultrasound if no clear portal of entry or if edema dominates over erythema.

evidence.citation: Pulia MS, Schwei RJ, Alexandridis R, et al. Validation of Thermal Imaging and the ALT-70 Prediction Model to Differentiate Cellulitis From Pseudocellulitis. JAMA Dermatol. 2024;160(5):511-517.
evidence.population: Adults presenting to ED with acute lower-extremity dermatologic symptoms, n=204, 92 with cellulitis
evidence.quote: specificity varied considerably (ALT-70, 22.0% [95% CI, 15.8%-28.1%]
evidence.reference_standard: Independent 6-physician consensus review of the case
evidence.target_condition: Lower-extremity cellulitis vs pseudocellulitis (ALT-70 model; asymmetry item weighted 3 points)

evidence.citation: Raff AB, Weng QY, Cohen JM, et al. A predictive model for diagnosis of lower extremity cellulitis: A cross-sectional study. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2017;76(4):618-625.e2.
evidence.population: Patients admitted via ED with a diagnosis of lower-extremity cellulitis, n=259, 2010-2012
evidence.quote: In total, 79 (30.5%) of 259 patients were misdiagnosed with lower extremity cellulitis
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis (cellulitis vs alternative diagnosis) after inpatient evaluation
evidence.target_condition: Lower-extremity cellulitis vs pseudocellulitis (ALT-70 derivation)

examine.how: Expose and compare both legs. Note whether erythema is unilateral (asymmetric) or bilateral, feel for warmth with the back of the hand against the contralateral limb, and trace the border (marking it with pen for follow-up). Check for a portal of entry (tinea, ulcer), tenderness, and disproportionate pain, crepitus or bullae.
examine.negative_finding: Bilateral symmetric erythema without fever, leukocytosis or tachycardia favors stasis dermatitis or other pseudocellulitis (ALT-70 0-2 points: >=83% pseudocellulitis); bilateral cellulitis is rare.
examine.pitfalls: ALT-70 is sensitive but only 22% specific in a prospective ED validation, so a 'positive' asymmetric leg still includes many DVT, gout, contact dermatitis and stasis cases; warmth is subjective; do not miss necrotizing infection (pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus).
examine.positive_finding: Unilateral warm, tender erythema, especially with leukocytosis, tachycardia or age >=70 (ALT-70 >=5 points), gives >=82% likelihood of true cellulitis in the derivation cohort. Asymmetry is the heaviest-weighted item (3 points).
examine.prerequisites: Both legs exposed; heart rate, temperature and WBC available if scoring ALT-70.
examine.title: Unilateral warm erythema with defined border (vs bilateral / stasis change)

examine.changes_what: Positive shifts unilateral/asymmetric edema toward lymphedema (consider lymphoscintigraphy, cancer/filarial causes); negative does not exclude it - still evaluate DVT and venous disease.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid forceps or forceful pinching on fragile or ulcerated skin.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a negative Stemmer sign to dismiss acute unilateral leg swelling - DVT must be excluded on its own merits; a positive sign in an obese or immobile patient is unreliable.
examine.escalation_warning: Rapidly progressive unilateral swelling, pain, warmth or erythema needs DVT and cellulitis/necrotizing infection assessment regardless of the Stemmer sign; new lymphedema in an adult warrants evaluation for pelvic/abdominal malignancy.

evidence.citation: Goss JA, Greene AK. Sensitivity and Specificity of the Stemmer Sign for Lymphedema: A Clinical Lymphoscintigraphic Study. Plast Reconstr Surg Glob Open. 2019.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results; same counts in Results paragraph 1 of PMC full text (PMC6635205)
evidence.population: 110 consecutive patients (mean age 35 y, range 1-88; 90 lower limb, 20 upper limb) referred to a tertiary Lymphedema Program, examined by a single senior surgeon
evidence.quote: positive Stemmer sign (n = 87) exhibited abnormal (n = 80) or normal (n = 7) lymphatic function by lymphoscintigraphy (sensitivity = 92%)
evidence.reference_standard: Lymphoscintigraphy (delayed tracer transit to inguinal/axillary nodes or dermal backflow = lymphedema)
evidence.target_condition: Lymphedema (primary or secondary, arm or leg)

evidence.citation: Jayaraj A, Raju S, May C, Pace N. The diagnostic unreliability of classic physical signs of lymphedema. J Vasc Surg Venous Lymphat Disord. 2019.
evidence.population: 436 swollen lower limbs (of 636 consecutive limbs, 12-month period) that underwent lymphoscintigraphy at a venous/lymphatic referral center; retrospective
evidence.quote: Sensitivity and specificity of clinical signs in predicting lymphoscintigraphy-confirmed lymphedema were 17% and 88%, respectively.
evidence.reference_standard: Lymphoscintigraphy scored on transit delay, dermal backflow, collaterals, uptake intensity and node counts
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: any classic clinical sign of lymphedema (dorsal hump, square toes, Kaposi-Stemmer sign, or nonpitting edema) - per-limb analysis

examine.how: With the patient standing (or supine), grasp the dorsal skin over the proximal phalanx of the second toe (or just proximal to the metatarsophalangeal joint; hand: index finger) between thumb and index finger and try to lift a thin skin fold. Compare with the contralateral limb.
examine.negative_finding: A pinchable fold argues against established lymphedema but does not exclude early (stage 1) or lean-patient lymphedema; venous edema, DVT and systemic causes remain possible.
examine.pitfalls: Obesity and immobility (e.g. neuromuscular disease) give false positives, and stage 1 disease or normal BMI give false negatives; chronic venous obstruction is the commonest cause of lymphedema-like signs with normal lymphoscintigraphy. Accuracy figures come from lymphedema-referral populations, not unselected edema.
examine.positive_finding: Positive (Kaposi-Stemmer sign) when the skin cannot be pinched into a fold because of thickened, fibrotic dorsal skin, indicating lymphedema (primary or secondary) rather than venous, cardiac, hepatic or renal edema.
examine.prerequisites: Foot exposed and clean; examine both feet; note BMI and any pitting.
examine.title: Stemmer sign: inability to pinch a skin fold at the base of the 2nd toe

examine.changes_what: Dullness + reduced fremitus: order CXR/POCUS for effusion. Dullness + increased fremitus/egophony: treat as consolidation. Normal fremitus at low pretest probability: may skip imaging.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for imaging when effusion or empyema would change management (e.g., febrile patient with suspected parapneumonic effusion).
examine.escalation_warning: Dullness with fever and hypoxia or with unilateral absent breath sounds and hemodynamic compromise warrants urgent imaging and drainage assessment.

evidence.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Straus SE. Does this patient have a pleural effusion? JAMA. 2009;301(3):309-317.
evidence.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms; 5 prospective studies, N=934
evidence.quote: dullness to conventional percussion was most accurate for diagnosing pleural effusion (summary positive likelihood ratio, 8.7; 95% confidence interval, 2.2-33.8)
evidence.target_condition: Pleural effusion (dullness to conventional percussion)

evidence.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Straus SE. Does this patient have a pleural effusion? JAMA. 2009;301(3):309-317.
evidence.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms; 5 prospective studies, N=934
evidence.quote: the absence of reduced tactile vocal fremitus made pleural effusion less likely (negative likelihood ratio, 0.21; 95% confidence interval, 0.12-0.37)
evidence.target_condition: Pleural effusion (absence of reduced tactile vocal fremitus)

evidence.citation: Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of Signs and Symptoms for the Diagnosis of Community-acquired Pneumonia: A Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
evidence.population: Adults with suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED)
evidence.quote: dullness to percussion (LR+ = 2.62, 95% CI = 1.14 to 5.30)
evidence.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia (dullness to percussion)

examine.how: Patient sitting; percuss the posterior and lateral chest from apex to base, comparing sides at each level, and mark where resonance changes to dull. Then ask the patient to say 'ninety-nine' while palpating the same sites with the ulnar hand edge to grade tactile fremitus. Auscultatory percussion: tap the manubrium while listening over the posterior chest.
examine.negative_finding: Normal (non-reduced) tactile fremitus lowers the probability of effusion (LR- 0.21) and may make radiography unnecessary when pretest probability is low.
examine.pitfalls: Small effusions (<300-500 mL) are missed; obesity, raised hemidiaphragm, and dense consolidation all produce dullness. Conventional percussion outperforms auscultatory percussion in pooled data.
examine.positive_finding: Stony dullness with reduced fremitus over a base strongly favors pleural effusion (pooled LR+ 8.7); dullness with increased fremitus and bronchial breathing favors consolidation (LR+ 2.6 for CAP).
examine.prerequisites: Bare skin, patient able to sit or lie lateral, quiet room.
examine.title: Dullness to percussion with decreased tactile fremitus (focal; conventional vs auscultatory percussion)

parsed.chief_complaint: new right calf swelling and pain
